title: MCP 2026-07-28: The Protocol's Biggest Revision Since Launch
content:
## Overview

In mid-2026, the Model Context Protocol shipped what its maintainers call the largest revision of the spec since its November 2024 launch. The new version — dated **MCP 2026-07-28** — reworks the protocol's core transport model and adds several extensions aimed at production-scale, multi-tenant deployments. A release candidate was announced May 21, 2026, with beta SDKs following on June 29, 2026.

This builds directly on the foundation described in [Tool Use & Agents](tool-use-and-agents): MCP standardizes how clients like Claude Code discover and call tools from servers. The 2026 revision is about making that standard scale.

---

## Stateless Core

The headline change is a **stateless architecture** that eliminates the old `initialize` handshake and protocol-level sessions entirely. Previously, an MCP client and server negotiated a session at connection time and had to keep talking to the same server instance for the life of that session — which meant sticky sessions and shared session state for any server run behind a load balancer.

Under the new core, each request carries everything the server needs to handle it. That means server infrastructure can scale horizontally behind **an ordinary round-robin load balancer** on standard HTTP infrastructure, with no sticky-session requirement and no shared session store. For teams running MCP servers at any real scale, this removes a whole category of infrastructure complexity.

---

## New Extensions

### MCP Apps
Servers can now describe **server-rendered UIs** through the MCP Apps extension, rather than being limited to returning text or JSON that a client has to render itself. This lets a server ship its own interactive surface — a form, a chart, a config panel — that renders consistently across any MCP Apps-compatible client.

### Tasks
The **Tasks extension** formalizes long-running operations. A client can kick off work that takes minutes or hours, get back a task handle immediately, and poll for status or fetch the result later — instead of holding a connection open or timing out. This matters for anything resembling a background agent run, a large data export, or a slow external API call fronted by an MCP server.

### Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA)
The EMA extension reached **stable** status in this revision. It aligns MCP's authorization model more closely with OAuth and OpenID Connect, and adds **URL-based client registration** — a user can hand a client a URL pointing at a metadata JSON document describing a server's credentials, streamlining onboarding. Combined with an org's identity provider, this enables "zero-touch" access: a user logs in once and reaches every MCP server the org has provisioned, rather than authenticating server-by-server.

### Sampling with Tools
A feature called **sampling with tools** lets an MCP server run its own agentic loop using the calling user's tokens, while the user retains control over what the server's loop is allowed to do. This reduces the amount of orchestration logic a client needs to write when a server-side task itself requires several rounds of tool use.

### Formal Deprecation Policy
The spec also picked up a formal deprecation framework, so future revisions can retire or replace features on a defined timeline — the explicit goal, per the maintainers, is to "evolve without breaking what you've built."

---

## Governance: MCP Joins the Linux Foundation

In **December 2025**, Anthropic donated MCP to the **Agentic AI Foundation**, a project under the Linux Foundation. This moved MCP from an Anthropic-led open standard to a vendor-neutral, community-governed one — the kind of governance transition that open protocols (HTTP, gRPC, OpenTelemetry) tend to go through once adoption is broad enough that no single vendor should hold the steering wheel. The 2026-07-28 revision is the first major spec release produced under this new governance structure.

---

## Why It Matters for Agent Builders

- **Ops simplicity:** stateless core means MCP servers can be deployed like any other stateless HTTP service — no custom session-affinity infrastructure.
- **Long-running work is now first-class:** the Tasks extension replaces ad hoc polling hacks that server authors previously had to invent themselves.
- **Enterprise auth gets simpler, not more complex:** EMA's zero-touch model reduces the number of times a user has to authenticate against different servers in a large org.
- **The protocol is no longer a single company's roadmap:** decisions now go through Linux Foundation governance, which should make the spec more predictable for anyone building a long-lived MCP server or client.
